blocks.html: Think of an ATM. You ask for ₹5,000 but your account holds only ₹2,000. The ATM does not switch off or freeze. It shows "Insufficient balance" and lets you try again. That is exactly what exception handling means: noticing a problem while the program is running and dealing with it gracefully.

blocks.html: A program can go wrong in three ways.

rows: Using a - b where you meant a + b
Division by zero, a file that is not found, an array index outside the array
The program itself, using exception handling

blocks.caption: Figure 1.2 · when each type of error is found

blocks.html: A syntax error breaks the grammar rules of C++. The compiler stops and does not create a program until you fix it.
A logical error compiles and runs, but it gives a wrong answer. The compiler cannot detect it.

blocks.code:
float average = m1 + m2 + m3 / 3;     // wrong: only m3 is divided by 3
float average = (m1 + m2 + m3) / 3.0; // correct

blocks.html: A runtime error happens while the program is running, usually because of bad input or a missing resource. In C++, many such problems can be reported as exceptions. If nobody handles an exception, the program ends abruptly by calling std::terminate() .

Key definition: An exception is an unusual event that happens while a program is running and stops the normal flow of instructions. Exception handling is the method of detecting such an event and responding to it, so that the program does not crash.

Important C++ fact: In C++, integer division by zero does not throw an exception automatically. It is undefined behaviour. The programmer must check for it and use throw to raise an exception. This is a key difference from Python, where ZeroDivisionError is raised automatically.

items.html: Stops crashes. The program stays running and shows a friendly message.
Keeps error code separate. The normal logic stays clean, and the error handling sits in its own block.
Sends errors upward. A function deep inside the program can report a problem to the function that called it.
Protects data. Files can be closed and memory freed even when something goes wrong.

An exception can be thrown inside a function and caught by the function that called it. This lets a small function report a problem without deciding how to show it to the user.

blocks.html: When an exception leaves a function, C++ destroys that function's local objects (calling their destructors) and goes back up the chain of calls until it finds a matching catch . This is called stack unwinding. For example, if main() calls f1() , f1() calls f2() , and f2() throws, then the locals of f2 and f1 are destroyed in turn until main() catches the exception.
One try can have many catch blocks, one for each type. C++ checks them from top to bottom and runs only the first one that matches.

items.html: catch(...) (three dots) is the catch-all handler. It catches an exception of any type.
It must always be the last catch . Otherwise the blocks after it can never run.

C++ does not convert types when it matches a catch : throw 5; will not be caught by catch(double) . The one exception to this rule is a derived class, which can be caught by a base-class handler (Section 1.6).

blocks.html: The C++ library provides ready-made exception classes in <stdexcept> and
<exception> . Each one has a member function what() that returns the error message.

rows: The base class of all standard exceptions

An index outside the range, e.g. vector.at(10) on a 5-element vector
An arithmetic result too large to store

blocks.html: Tip: Always catch exception objects by reference (const out_of_range& e ). This avoids making a copy and keeps the correct derived type.
You can create your own exception class. The best way is to derive it from
std::exception (or from runtime_error ) and override what() .

blocks.code:
Withdrawn: 500, Left: 1500
Error: Insufficient balance in account

blocks.html: Order rule: When you catch both a derived class and its base class, put the derived class first. If catch(const exception&) comes first, it catches everything, and catch(const InsufficientBalance&) will never run.
A catch block can do part of the work (such as writing a log) and then pass the same exception upward with a plain throw; .

C++ has no finally block. It uses a stronger idea called RAII (Resource Acquisition Is Initialization): a resource is wrapped in an object, and the object's destructor releases it. Destructors always run during stack unwinding, so the cleanup happens whether or not an exception occurs.

items.html: Errors are of three types: syntax (found by the compiler), logical (wrong output), and runtime (happen while the program runs).
An exception is an unusual event at runtime that breaks the normal flow of a program.
